en: The Sūtra on King Siṃha-sauḍasa’s Abstinence from Meat, Spoken by the Buddha;
translated by the Da Tang Śramaṇa Jñānagupta.
I recall that in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a king named Sauḍasa!
Once, that king went out on an excursion to the mountains, with his ministers and retinue hunting insects and beasts.
Suddenly, thunder, hail, and a fierce wind arose;
the people scattered in total alarm, while the king alone fled into the deep forest. Reaching a river to rest, he was without any companion.
A female lioness dwelling in the mountain thickets saw the King sitting alone and approached his person.
Due to the evil karma and past conditions of sentient beings, they undergo immeasurable suffering by being reborn in hell.
The King and the lion shared a karmic affinity from former lives; their passions arose together and they united.
Having for many kalpas eaten meat and killed living beings, due to these long-standing habits he entered the womb of a lion.
Thus he was born with a human body and a lion’s head, a man with spotted feet like the king of beasts.
Having grown up with great speed and extreme vigor, he asked his mother,
"Whose lineage am I?
His mother, Siṃhī, replied to her son:
"Your father is King Suprabuddha of the kingdom of Kāśī.
Having heard this, the son went quickly to seek him out at the place of his father, the king of Magadha.
He presented himself and fully explained the circumstances of his journey; upon hearing this, the king realized the truth for himself and took him as his son."
However, because his father the King had grown old and infirm, he ascended the tower and was consecrated as king;
he was named Siṃhasudāsa, and from the palace he governed the state affairs and ruled over his ministers and subjects.
Due to the successive accumulation of evil habits as a lion, for many kalpas he ate flesh and harmed sentient beings;
though he now dwells as a king of men, he does not eat grain, consuming only birds, beasts, and insects from water and land.
As the time for presenting the various meats drew near, a dog seized a beast’s meat and carried it off.
Fearing the King’s execution, the kitchen cook ran out to seize a small infant;
he secretly severed its head, neck, hands, and feet, boiled them whole in a cauldron, and presented them to the King.
The king found the meat most delicious and grew to crave its flavor as one longs for burning incense.
The king asked the chief cook, "What kind of meat is this?
The cook, terrified, explained everything to the king; the king pardoned his crime and told him not to grieve, ordering that this same meat be served to him every day.
Having received the Great King’s command, the cook changed his attire and daily stole others' children;
for many years he secretly abducted their sons and daughters, acting like a rākṣasa and like a hawk.
The people within the realm all observed mourning; distressed by the loss of their children, they were each filled with terror.
Pairs of them held hands and questioned one another, their breath choked as they had nowhere to appeal to the August Heaven.
The townspeople captured the thief while he was cooking; the thief pleaded that he had acted without his own consent.
When the people heard this, they petitioned the king to offer counsel. Upon hearing this, the king became enraged and rebuked him with great wrath:
"Until now, you have been ordered to secretly serve me the flesh of infants; from this day forward, you shall provide one portion for yourself alone."
Relatives, ministers, and subjects ate in succession, like sheep being led away from within a pen;
the entire kingdom was filled with despair and had no one to appeal to, so they gathered before the royal palace, desiring to remove the king.
The king ascended the high terrace and prayed to the gods and spirits:

"I pray that you grant me wings to fly away and escape this calamity; if I may obtain wings to soar to all quarters, I shall take the heads of the kings of a hundred nations as offerings to the mountain deity."
Due to the evil habit of being a fierce lion, he instantly grew wings and flew to seize various kings, imprisoning them upon high peaks and steep cliffs.
Having already captured ninety-nine kings, he lacked but one king for his sacrifice; the lion descended once more to search for him.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva king of Rājagṛha named Śruticandra, who had bathed in the garden;
King Siṃhadarśana saw him sitting upon a jade throne and descended to seize his right arm, intending to capture and lead him away.
At that time, King Śruticandra wept, and Siṃha asked the king why he was crying.
"I have heard, Great King, that you possess courageous wisdom; that a Bodhisattva disregards body, life, and wealth."
"If one should thus practice patience, why endure suffering and grief without self-mastery?
Hearing this, Candraprabha replied to the King-Siṃha:
"All sorrow and suffering do not exceed compassion; one should cultivate the great compassion of a Bodhisattva."
I now grieve for those kings of the hundred lands, who were lords of the world in noble splendor throughout their lives, yet today are imprisoned with their lives at its end;
I also grieve for the hundred lands seeking the Buddha-dharma, who invited a Dharma Master from afar,
but have not yet had the chance to hear the Dharma or receive his personal instruction, while the people of the nation thirst and look up to him, having never heard it before.
"Please grant me seven days to make offerings to the Triple Gem and listen to the sound of the Dharma;
I shall assemble my ministers to entrust them with the Dharma, and on the eighth day, I shall come myself to welcome Your Majesty."
Because this Bodhisattva was free from deceit and falsehood, he granted the lion king a period of seven days;
on the eighth day, hearing that the moon had risen, he left the city to go out and meet the lion king, abandoning his own body as an offering.
At that time, Siṃha appeared like a cloud; seizing and bringing forth Śruticandra, he presented him before the assembly.
Siṃha asked the king:
"Are you not afraid?"
"Who dares to come before me like the King of Beasts?
Hearing this, Moon replied to the king, the lion:
"This body, false and illusory, I offer to Your Majesty; I would rather sacrifice hundreds of thousands of lives, bodies, and wealth than violate my previous word or fail your appointment."
With a gentle countenance and a pleasant expression, he spoke with skillful means:
“Listen for a moment as I explain the causal conditions.
If you wish to sacrifice to heterodox spirits and ghosts, the various classes of benevolent deities will bring calamity upon you.”
The worthy sages of the Buddha-fields in the ten directions— For many kalpas you have not heard their names again.
This body is a false combination of causes and conditions; Life is like a flash of lightning, with no staying power.
The five faculties and six consciousnesses have no self or person; The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and touch serve as their causes.
Like illusory transformations that manifest various forms, sentient beings’ deluded thoughts grasp them as real;
yet from head to foot, when this body is examined, not a single thing is permanent.
Like bubbles upon water that perish in an instant, the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are likewise impermanent.
Although you now nourish your body with flesh, in the end you will have no refuge and no path of virtue;
having killed countless beings and devoured their meat, you shall suffer in turn within the evil realms.
At that time, having heard the immeasurable verses of Śruticandra, he exhorted King Siṃhaśuddhā;
having heard them, Siṃha gradually turned his mind and listened to the true nature of non-self.
The Lion asked the King:
"By what means may one perform sacrifices without incurring sin and thereby please the gods?
Śrutakarṇa replied:
“Prepare vegetarian delicacies; offer pure food as a sacrifice to the gods.
As the lion commands, sacrifice to the mountain deities; bestow your body as an offering to King Śrutaviśruta.
All those kings imprisoned within the mountains shall likewise be entrusted to Śrutaviśruta.”
Having heard this, each returned to their own kingdom and governed the people according to the former laws;
together with King Siṃhasaudāsa, they settled in their original palace in Magadha.
There, they united the ministers and the myriad subjects, and throughout the entire nation, the eating of meat was forbidden and killing was ceased.
At that time, Wencheng (Moon of Hearing) made this great vow:
"May all living beings be liberated, And may these kings together attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the sublime Dharma bestowed upon King Siṃha, I pray that his heavy transgressions may vanish like clouds."
He further reflected:

"In the past, incalculable eons ago, Śakra Devānām Indra was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace; due to the residual habit of eating meat in the past, he transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a dove."
At that time, I was a king named Śibi; out of compassion for the pigeon, I weighed my own body and cut off my flesh to ransom its life.
That King Śibi was none other than myself. Hereafter, I shall become a king named Śruticandra.
As for the one who was Śakra, transformed into a hawk at that time, he shall later become a king named Siṃhaśuddha.

"If even Śakra, because he tested me, was still reborn in the evil realms, how much more so for other sentient beings who, lacking shame, are solely intent on killing, devouring flesh and blood without ever reaching satiety?
Since all sentient beings have, from time immemorial, never failed to be our parents or relatives, and easily take birth as birds and beasts, how can we bear to eat them?"
Those who eat meat have been born as birds and beasts throughout kalpas, devouring the flesh and blood of others in a cycle of mutual retribution for their lives.
If one is born among humans yet remains devoted to killing and consuming meat, upon death they will fall into the Avīci Hell without a moment's respite.
If a person can sever the habit of eating meat for even a single lifetime, they shall never again consume it until they attain Buddhahood.
The Sūtra on King Siṃhasudāsa’s Abstinence from Meat Spoken by the Buddha.
